newsitem.title: UK: Losers as well as winners among UK soccer stocks.
newsitem.headline: Losers as well as winners among UK soccer stocks.

text.p: Manchester United, Newcastle United and now Aston Villa.
The London Stock Exchange has become a second home to UK soccer clubs but share analysts said on Friday there could be losers as well as winners in the flotation game.
Birmingham-based Villa unveiled plans on Thursday for a share issue to raise more than 15 million pounds ($24.5 million) and value the club at 125 million pounds.
On Friday, Scotland's Heart of Midlothian announced it had raised five million pounds in a share placing and would join the stock market next month, valued at a more modest 14 million pounds.
Villa and Hearts take the number of soccer clubs listed on the full stock market or London's junior Alternative Investment Market to 17, the soccer sector now being worth some 1.5 billion pounds.
More English clubs are waiting in the wings and Italian giants such as AC Milan and Juventus are reported to be considering the idea of a London listing.

English soccer, which appeared in terminal decline in the 1980s, has been transformed in the past few years thanks largely to a huge cash injection from the Rupert Murdoch-controlled pay television group BSkyB Plc.

The money has helped to fund the import of top foreign players and pay for greatly improved facilities, which in turn has helped to reduce hooliganism at matches. Clubs have caught the entrepreneurial spirit, tightening up their management structures and building up their merchandising arms.

The role model has been Manchester United, English league champions and a business worth more than 400 million pounds and employing some 450 full-time staff. But as more and more clubs come to the market, the task for investors large and small is to spot the potential winners.
"It's very much the search for quality players, those clubs that can definitely stay in the English premier league," said Nigel Hawkins of brokerage Yamaichi Securities.

His point was underlined by a sharp fall on Friday in shares in Sunderland Plc, which lost 20p to 497.5p. Sunderland shares were floated at 585p in December and were worth over seven pounds at one point but have dipped in recent weeks as the threat of relegation from the big money premier leahue has grown.

This weekend's relegation battle against north-east neighbours Middlesbrough is crucial in their struggle for survival. Nick Batram of brokers Greig, Middleton believes that the market has not yet reached saturation point, saying that the sector could grow to embrace as many as 25 clubs. But he said that an air of reality has come into valuations in recent weeks, replacing euphoria about the potential income from pay-per-view television.
"The choice is such now that investors are more aggressive in their approach to pricing. It is a sign of the sector maturing," he said. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
